Definition & the Difference Quotient

▸ Difference quotient The average rate of change of f over the interval from x to x + h: [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h . Geometrically, this is the slope of the secant line through two points on the curve.

▸ The derivative f′(x) = lim h→0 [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h . As h shrinks to 0, the secant line becomes the tangent line, and its slope is the derivative — the instantaneous rate of change.

Power, Constant & Sum Rules

The Core Rules — The power rule is "bring the exponent down front, then knock it down by one." Think of the exponent jumping down to become a multiplier and leaving behind a value one…

Why the Constant Rule Makes Sense — A constant function like f(x) = 7 is a flat horizontal line. Its slope is 0 everywhere — so its derivative is 0. Constants vanish under differentiation.

▸ Quotient rule d/dx[f/g] = (f′·g − f·g′) / g² . The order of the subtraction matters: it is "derivative of top times bottom, minus top times derivative of bottom, all over bottom squared."

▸ Chain rule d/dx[f(g(x))] = f′(g(x)) · g′(x) . "Derivative of the outside (with the inside left in place), times the derivative of the inside."

Linear Approximation & Differentials

▸ Linear approximation Near x = a, f(x) ≈ L(x) = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a) . This is just the equation of the tangent line at a, used as a stand-in for f.

▸ Differential If y = f(x), the differential is dy = f′(x) · dx . It estimates the change in y produced by a small change dx in x — the same idea as linear approximation, written in change-language.

Extrema & Critical Points

▸ Local (relative) extrema A local maximum is a point higher than its immediate neighbors; a local minimum is lower than its neighbors. Absolute extrema are the highest/lowest over the entire domain or interval.

▸ Critical point A point in the domain where f′(x) = 0 or f′(x) is undefined . All local extrema occur at critical points (though not every critical point is an extremum).

The Mean Value Theorem

▸ Mean Value Theorem If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there exists at least one c in (a, b) where f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)] / (b − a) — the instantaneous slope equals the average slope.

Concavity & Curve Sketching

▸ Concavity Concave up (holds water, ∪-shaped): f″(x) > 0. Concave down (spills water, ∩-shaped): f″(x) < 0. An inflection point is where concavity switches (f″ = 0 and changes sign).

Optimization

The Strategy — You have a fixed length of fence and want to enclose the biggest possible yard. Stretch it long and thin and the area is tiny; make it a balanced shape and the area…

L'Hopital's Rule

▸ L'Hopital's Rule If lim f(x)/g(x) has the form 0/0 or ∞/∞, then lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f′(x)/g′(x) , provided the second limit exists. Differentiate numerator and denominator independently — this is not the quotient rule.

📋 The Integral

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Antiderivatives & Indefinite Integrals

▸ Antiderivative F is an antiderivative of f if F′(x) = f(x). Since the derivative of any constant is 0, antiderivatives come in a family differing by a constant: we write ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C .

Riemann Sums & the Definite Integral

▸ Riemann sum An approximation of area by rectangles: Σ f(xᵢ)·Δx , where Δx is each rectangle's width and f(xᵢ) is its height. More, thinner rectangles give a better estimate.

▸ Definite integral ∫ a b f(x) dx = the limit of Riemann sums as Δx → 0 = the exact signed area between the curve and the x-axis from a to b. Unlike the indefinite integral, it is a number , not a function.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

▸ FTC Part 1 If F(x) = ∫ a x f(t) dt, then F′(x) = f(x) . Differentiating an accumulation function returns the integrand — differentiation undoes integration.

▸ FTC Part 2 (Evaluation) If F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫ a b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) . To find a definite integral, find an antiderivative and subtract its values at the endpoints.

Substitution (u-substitution)

▸ u-substitution To integrate f(g(x))·g′(x) dx, let u = g(x) , so du = g′(x) dx . The integral becomes ∫ f(u) du — usually something basic. Integrate in u, then substitute x back.

Area Between Curves

▸ Area between curves If f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], the area between them is ∫ a b [f(x) − g(x)] dx — the integral of (top − bottom).

The trap is reading off the constant 4 or the root x = 0.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "x = 0 is a root of f, not a place where the slope 2x - 4 vanishes.", "1": "x = -2 flips the sign when solving 2x = 4.", "2": "x = 4 is the other root of f(x) = x^2 - 4x, not the critical point."}}, {"id": "c4", "topic": "Compute", "text": "For f(x) = x^2 on [0, 2], the MVT value c is:", "options": ["1", "1.5", "0", "2"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Average slope 2; f prime(c)=2c=2 -> c = 1.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"1": "1.5 is the midpoint of [0, 2], but the MVT point is where 2c equals the average slope 2.", "2": "0 is the left endpoint, and f'(0) = 0, not the average slope 2.", "3": "2 is the right endpoint, where f'(2) = 4, not 2."}}, {"id": "c4_d2", "topic": "Example", "text": "For f(x) = x^3, the inflection point is at:", "options": ["x = -1", "x = 0", "x = 1", "local min"], "correct": 1, "explain": "f prime prime = 6x changes sign at x = 0.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "x = -1 has f'' = -6, negative on both sides nearby, so no sign change occurs there.", "2": "x = 1 has f'' = 6, again with no sign change.", "3": "x^3 has no local minimum; its slope never changes sign."}}, {"id": "c2_d2", "topic": "Square", "text": "The maximum-area rectangle with perimeter 20 is:", "options": ["2 by 8", "1 by 9", "5 by 5", "4 by 6"], "correct": 2, "explain": "With perimeter 20, x + y = 10 and A = x(10 - x). The trap is using the quotient rule instead of differentiating each part.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "0 reads the numerator's zero and ignores that the denominator vanishes too.", "1": "sin x stays bounded by 1, so the quotient cannot blow up.", "2": "0/0 is indeterminate, not undefined: the limit exists and equals 1."}}, {"id": "c4_d3", "topic": "Plug in", "text": "If r = 3 and dr/dt = 2, then dA/dt equals:", "options": ["9 pi", "6 pi", "18 pi", "12 pi"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Differentiate A = pi r^2 with respect to t: dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt = 2 pi (3)(2) = 12 pi. The trap is using pi r^2 = 9 pi, the area, instead of the rate.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "9 pi is the area pi r^2 at r = 3, not the rate at which it grows.", "1": "6 pi drops the factor 2 or one of r and dr/dt from 2 pi r dr/dt.", "2": "18 pi multiplies pi r^2 by dr/dt instead of differentiating r^2 first."}}, {"id": "c4_d4", "topic": "Basis", "text": "Linear approximation uses the:", "options": ["second derivative", "secant line", "tangent line", "area"], "correct": 2, "explain": "It replaces the curve by its tangent line near a.", "__rebal": 1, "distractors": {"0": "The second derivative measures concavity; linearization needs only the first derivative.", "1": "The secant line joins two points; the linearization uses the tangent at one point.", "3": "Area comes from integration and has no role in a tangent-line estimate."}}, {"id": "d1", "topic": "Find", "text": "For f(x) = x^2 - 6x, the critical point is at:", "options": ["x = 0", "x = 6", "x = -3", "x = 3"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Set f'(x) = 2x - 6 = 0, which gives x = 3. That is where the parabola turns.
